recommendation.text: The committee voted unanimously (9 yes, 0 no, 0 abstain) that dabigatran should be approved for reduction of stroke and non-CNS systemic embolism in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation.

quote.quote: The Committee voted on the question: "Should dabigatran be approved for the reduction of stroke and non-CNS systemic embolism in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation?" The vote was "yes" = 9, "no" = 0, "abstain" = 0.

linkages.concern: At the advisory committee a suggestion was made to also approve the lower 110-mg dose, out of concern that patients and physicians would observe bleeding on the 150-mg dose and stop therapy if no lower dose were available; the committee was split fairly evenly on whether to market one dose (150 mg only) or both.
linkages.change: FDA approved only the 150-mg strength and declined to market the 110-mg dose.

concern_quote.quote: A suggestion was made at the Advisory Committee to approve the 110-mg dose anyway. The rationale was that patients and physicians are going to observe bleeding on the 150-mg dose, and if they do not have a lower dose, they will stop therapy.

change_quote.quote: My decision to approve only the 150-mg strength was a difficult one, based largely on the views of the Division, and my concern about loss of efficacy in many thousands of patients who would inappropriately opt for the lower dose, if available.

summary: An advisory committee (the Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee) was convened on September 20, 2010, and voted unanimously (9-0-0) that dabigatran should be approved for reduction of stroke and systemic embolism in non-valvular atrial fibrillation. The committee's substantive debate centered on dose: it was split fairly evenly on whether to market both the 150-mg and 110-mg doses or only 150 mg, and some members suggested approving the 110-mg dose. FDA ultimately approved only the 150-mg strength (adding a 75-mg strength for severe renal impairment), reasoning that availability of a lower dose would lead many patients to inappropriately lose efficacy.
